system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and odynophagia, following a recent hospitalization for respiratory symptoms. She has a complex history including prior tracheal cancer treated with radiation, which likely contributed to esophageal stricture and ulceration. A barium swallow revealed a 3 cm esophageal stricture that prevented passage of a 12-mm tablet, and EGD confirmed severe radiation-related esophagitis with an ulcer and nodule, both biopsied. Due to inflammation, dilation was deferred. She was treated empirically for candidal esophagitis with fluconazole and started on high-dose pantoprazole. Her viral upper respiratory infection resolved with supportive care, and her abdominal symptoms improved with antiemetics and bowel management. Prednisone was adjusted for rheumatoid arthritis flare, and her asthma, heart failure, and hypertension were managed. She was discharged home with services on a prednisone taper, pantoprazole, fluconazole, and follow-up plans for biopsy results and GI reevaluation.
problems: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of breast
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung

thickening of the posterior wall of the right main bronchus, is also new.  A
16 x 14 mm right lower paratracheal lymph node, 2:14, is difficult to discern
on any prior CT scans, but may be new also.

Heart is mildly enlarged, unchanged.  There is no pericardial effusion.  Small
right pleural effusion has increased.  This study is not designed for
subdiaphragmatic diagnosis, but shows no adrenal mass.  It is not appropriate
for liver evaluation.

Radiation fibrosis in the paramediastinal left upper lobe, and subpleural
aspect of the right anterior lung are stable.  There is new mild peribronchial
opacification in the superior segment of the left lower lobe.  Given the
severe esophagitis and the possibility of tumor recurrence interfering with
swallowing, the most likely explanation for this is aspiration.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Severe wall thickening, mid esophagus, probably esophagitis.  Peritracheal
and peribronchial soft tissue thickening and increase in subcarinal right
lower paraesophageal lymph node size could also be radiation effect, but is
indistinguishable from recurrent infiltrating tumor.  Distortion of the lower
tracheal lumen could be due to scarring, but needs to be kept in mind as a
possible stricture or ulceration, in turn raising the possibility of a
recurrent tracheal carcinoma.

Findings were discussed by telephone with the resident physician caring for
this patient at the time of dictation.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with a complicated past medical history
including breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer and tracheal cancer, now
status post XRT and chemo with complication with esophagitis, dysphagia and
odynophagia.  Please place G-tube.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___ (resident), Dr. ___ (attending).  Dr.
___ attending radiologist, was present throughout the procedure.

SEDATION:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
fentanyl and Versed throughout the total intra-service time of 1 hour 20
minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored.  75 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed were used. 

PROCEDURE TECHNIQUE:  Signed informed written consent was obtained prior to
the procedure.  The patient was placed supine on the angiographic table.  An
NG tube was initially inserted under fluoroscopic guidance. The left abdomen
was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  The liver edge was
marked using ultrasound. Glucagon was administered prior to the procedure.

Under fluoroscopic guidance, a site was selected overlying the anterior
abdominal wall corresponding to the stomach below.  Lateral fluoroscopic
images were obtained to ensure no overlying bowel.  The stomach continued to
be insufflated through an NG tube.  1% lidocaine was used for topical
anesthesia.  Three T-fasteners were deployed within the gastric lumen.  The
position was confirmed by injection of contrast and aspiration of air.  A
19-gauge needle was then advanced into the stomach until air was aspirated. 
Contrast was then injected to ensure correct positioning.  A ___ wire was
advanced through the 19-gauge needle and curled within the stomach as seen on
fluoroscopic images.  The needle was then exchanged for a dilator which was
subsequently exchanged for a 6 ___ sheath.  A Kumpe catheter was then
advanced through the sheath and directed towards the pylorus.  A Glidewire was
exchanged for the ___ wire and with subsequent manipulation we were able
to advance both the Kumpe and the Glidewire into the duodenum and subsequently
into the jejunum.  Contrast was then injected to ensure positioning within the
jejunum.  The ___ wire was exchanged for an Amplatz wire.  The sheath and
Kumpe catheter were then removed.  After successful dilations with a 12 ___
dilator, a 14 ___ peel-away sheath with dilator was introduced over the
Amplatz wire. The dilator was removed and over the Amplatz wire, the 14 ___
___ tube was then advanced with fluoroscopic guidance.  ___ tube tip was
seen within the jejunum and the Amplatz and peel-away sheath were subsequently
removed.  Contrast was then injected ensuring the placement within the
jejunum.  The loop was formed and locked.  The feeding tube was secured to the
skin using 0 silk sutures and a Flexi-Trak.  The site was dressed.  There were
no post-procedure complications.  The NG tube was removed.

IMPRESSION:  Successful placement of a 14 ___ ___ tube with tip
terminating in the jejunum.  No immediate complications.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST, ___

HISTORY:  Cough and productive sputum.  On prednisone.

IMPRESSION:  AP and lateral chest compared to ___.

Small right hemithorax and distortion of the hilus reflect prior surgery. 
Lung periphery is clear.  The heart is mildly enlarged.  No appreciable
pleural effusion.

INDICATION:  ___ female with acute nausea, vomiting and abdominal
pain.  Evaluate for bowel obstruction.

EXAMINATION:  Supine and erect abdominal radiographs.

COMPARISONS:  ___.

FINDINGS:  A percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube remains in stable standard
position.  Clips overlie the mid abdomen.  There is a medium amount of stool
most prominent within the right colon.  There is a non-obstructive bowel gas
pattern.  There is no evidence of pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum or portal
venous air.  There are no abnormal soft tissue calcifications or radiopaque
foreign bodies.  The visualized osseous structures are intact.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Gastrojejunostomy tube in standard position.
2.  Non-obstructive bowel gas pattern. Medium degree of fecal loading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mrs. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were admitted last night with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been having trouble swallowing—both liquids and solids. It feels like food gets stuck in my chest. And every time I swallow, it burns and hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like odynophagia and dysphagia. You mentioned vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I vomit a lot after trying to eat. I haven’t been eating much at all lately because it just makes everything worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of tracheal cancer and radiation therapy, this is likely related to radiation damage to your esophagus—what we call radiation esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not cancer coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping an eye on that. A recent CT showed thickening in your esophagus, which could be inflammation or possibly tumor recurrence. But right now, the signs point more toward severe esophagitis from prior radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an EGD a few weeks ago. They saw a stricture and ulcers, but couldn’t dilate it because of too much inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I reviewed your records. The biopsy showed radiation changes, no HSV, CMV, or fungal infection. You completed a course of fluconazole, so we won’t repeat that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m still not getting better. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflammation is still active. We’ve started you on a dissolving lansoprazole since you’ve had trouble swallowing pills. We’re also adding sucralfate and reglan to help coat the esophagus and improve motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those going to help with the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll help protect the lining and reduce irritation. For pain, we’re continuing your MS Contin and will use IV morphine as needed. We want to keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been coughing more—sometimes with phlegm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a low-grade fever yesterday and a productive cough. Your chest X-ray was clear, and urine culture was negative. We think it’s viral tracheobronchitis, possibly from radiation effects or a mild infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want antibiotics unless I really need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. No signs of bacterial pneumonia, and your fever resolved on its own. We’ll stick with supportive care—benzonatate for the cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your CT scan from yesterday. It shows worsening esophageal wall thickening, consistent with progressive esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to tell definitively on imaging. The changes could be from inflammation or recurrence. But given your prior biopsies, we’re leaning toward radiation injury for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI was consulted. Because of the severe ulceration, they don’t recommend dilation now—it could cause a tear. Instead, they suggest placing a feeding tube to let your esophagus heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A feeding tube? I was hoping to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with your dysphagia and vomiting, you’re not getting enough nutrition. The tube will help you heal and prevent further weight loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not necessarily. Once the inflammation improves, we can reassess for dilation and possibly remove it. This is a temporary support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When would it be placed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow morning, guided by X-ray. The procedure is called a PEJ—percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy. It goes directly into your small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your PEJ tube was placed successfully this morning. It’s in the right spot, and we’ve started tube feeds at a slow rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel some pain around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. There will be discomfort for a few weeks as the tract heals. We’ll keep your pain managed with your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been constipated. Haven’t had a bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The KUB showed moderate stool buildup. We’ve prescribed senna and docusate. You’ve refused them so far—can we start today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess so. I just hate being dependent on laxatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it’s important to prevent pain and bloating. We’ll use the lowest effective dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved since the tube was placed. You haven’t vomited in over 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a relief. But I still have burning in my chest when I swallow saliva.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from the esophagitis. We’re continuing high-dose pantoprazole and sucralfate. Healing takes time—weeks, not days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on prednisone for my arthritis, but I never started the taper after my last hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting the taper now—3 tablets a day for 3 days, then gradually down. Stopping steroids suddenly can be dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding nortriptyline at night for nerve pain. It may also help with sleep and chronic pain from fibromyalgia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, especially at first. That’s actually helpful at bedtime. We’ll start low and go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your hemoglobin has been dropping—from 10.2 to 8.1. But no sign of bleeding. Likely due to chronic disease and poor intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your levels are stable, and you’re not symptomatic. With tube feeds, your nutrition should improve, and your blood counts may recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cough is still there, but your repeat chest X-ray is clear. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still producing phlegm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, it could be from chronic bronchitis or post-radiation changes. We’ll continue guaifenesin to help loosen secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows your feeding tube is in good position and no obstruction. Stool load is improving since you started the laxatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain around the tube is a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ve increased your morning MS Contin to 30mg for better pain control. But we can’t go higher—you got confused the last time we tried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want to be out of it. I’d rather have some pain than be confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, your symptoms are controlled, and you’re tolerating tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will my care be like at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with visiting nurses. They’ll help with tube care, feeding, and meds. You’ll continue pantoprazole, sucralfate, and a short course of fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I already finished fluconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did, but we’re giving a short 9-day course as a precaution. Also, your prednisone taper continues—follow the new schedule exactly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll receive tube feeds overnight—120 mL per hour for 14 hours. Flush with water before and after. You can still take meds by mouth or through the tube, except your MS Contin—don’t crush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I can’t swallow it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. Don’t crush or cut it. We may need to adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI in two weeks. They’ll reassess for possible dilation. Keep taking care of the tube site and report any redness, swelling, or leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some discomfort, but I understand it will take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tube site will hurt for a few more weeks. But you’re on the right path. We’ll support you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I feel prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted for intractable nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dysphagia, and odynophagia, all stemming from severe radiation esophagitis related to prior treatment for tracheal cancer. Despite a recent hospitalization and treatment with high-dose pantoprazole and fluconazole, her symptoms progressed, leading to poor oral intake and dehydration. A CT scan showed worsening esophageal wall thickening, and GI consultation confirmed she was not a candidate for dilation due to severe ulceration. A percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy (PEJ) tube was placed to enable enteral feeding and allow the esophagus to heal. Her nausea and vomiting resolved post-procedure, and pain was managed with adjusted opioid dosing. A prednisone taper was initiated for rheumatoid arthritis, and nortriptyline was started for neuropathic pain. She was discharged home with nursing services, a detailed medication regimen, and plans for outpatient GI follow-up to reassess for dilation in several weeks.
